title: Leo Watson, Scatman Crothers and the Spirits of Rhythm
summary: Dickenson recorded with Scatman Crothers and Leo Watson, a trombonist who mainly sang and kept him laughing; Morgenstern praises Leo's As Long As I Live.

story.theme_name: Singers and the musicians who accompanied them

blocks.x: There's another guy, Scatman Crothers, too. I think he's a Leo Watson man.
Well, you recorded with him.
Yeah, I recorded with both of them.
Dickenson - 122
I heard you say once that Leo was quite a trombone player, too.
Yeah, he was a trombone player.
But he never really featured it?
No, singing, that was his main thing. I forget what band he was with. It was some big band.
Krupa for a while.
Was it Jan Savitt or something?
He was with Gene Krupa for a while.
Was it Gene Krupa?
Yes.
I thought it was Jan Savitt or something like that.
'Bon Bon' was with Jan Savitt.
Oh, they did 'Bon Bon.' But didn't 'Bon Bon' [Tunnell] fall (?) into something?
Could be. He might have been. He probably never made any records. Because he made some records with Gene -- 'Nagasaki,' which is pretty wild.
Yeah, he was a pretty wild guy. He'd keep you laughing. Every time I made a record with him, I had to laugh all the time I was playing. Heh, he was funny.
But also, he sang some beautiful musical things. I've got a record of his of 'As Long As I Live' with The Spirits
Dickenson - 123
of Rhythm.
Oh yeah?

And he takes a long... He takes a chorus on there, with just a little humming in the background. And it's beautiful. It's really... You could play that on an instrument, and it would be a lovely song.
I haven't heard that.
I'll put it on the tape for you.
Okay.
It sounds like Lester a little bit, before... You know, it's 1935 or something. He comes in so nice.
Mmm-hmm.
